claims.text: The target nanoparticles are noble-metal-based high-entropy alloys containing more than five elements.
The initial material is a single-phase solid solution.
Crystal-structure selection is governed by an interplay of thermodynamic driving forces, kinetic barriers, and processing conditions.
Experimental synthesis combined with computational modeling of phase diagrams and thermodynamics can control formation and crystal-structure selection.
Heating and cooling rates will be varied in a controlled manner.
Composition will be varied in a controlled manner.
Changing heating rate, cooling rate, and composition modulates thermodynamic driving forces and kinetic barriers.
The relevant structural mediators include free-energy landscapes and diffusion coefficients.
Thermodynamic driving forces and kinetic barriers influence phase separation.
Thermodynamic driving forces and kinetic barriers influence elemental segregation.
Thermodynamic driving forces and kinetic barriers influence nanoparticle morphology.
The resulting phase-separation, segregation, and morphology behavior leads to selection of a specific crystal structure.
Optimizing processing conditions and composition will increase the yield of single-phase solid-solution nanoparticles with controlled crystal structure by 20% relative to baseline.
The compositional boundary is limited to alloys containing more than five elements.
The processing boundary is synthesis involving rapid heating and cooling.
The hypothesis is falsified if optimization does not increase the yield of single-phase nanoparticles with controlled crystal structure by at least 10% relative to baseline.
